summary: DMARC lets domains state policies for email validation, disposition and reporting, but it can cause interoperability problems when messages do not flow directly from the author's domain to the receiver, such as through mailing lists. This informational document describes these issues and discusses possible mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: When a domain asks that its mail be rejected unless it passes a security check, mail that has been forwarded or altered on the way can fail that check and be blocked. This document explains why that happens and what mail operators can do about it.

questions: why does dmarc break mailing lists
what is an indirect email flow
how to fix dmarc with mailing lists
what is identifier alignment in dmarc
subtitle: Why strict DMARC policies break mailing lists, forwarders and other mail that does not travel straight from author to reader.

tldr.problem: DMARC lets a domain say how its mail should be treated, and it works by checking that the domain that signed the message matches the domain in the From header. Mail that is forwarded, resent or rewritten along the way breaks that match.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies the causes, including identifier alignment, forwarding and message modification, walks through the parts of the mail architecture where each arises, and lists the mitigations operators are already using.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational analysis with no mechanism of its own: it gives senders, receivers, re-senders and mailing lists a set of practical options and points to a handful of unfinished Internet-Drafts for longer-term solutions.

today: RFC 7960 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the IETF analysis of DMARC's effect on indirect email flows. It defines no mechanism of its own, and it notes that the mitigations it lists may in some cases violate conventions or expectations, and that practices in use may or may not be best practices as future standards evolve.

sections.title: The Problem in One Page
sections.content:
DMARC, defined in RFC 7489, introduces a mechanism for expressing domain-level policies and preferences for message validation, disposition and reporting. The mechanism, especially when employed with restrictive policies, encounters several different types of interoperability issue because of third-party message sourcing, message transformation or rerouting. In particular, DMARC with restrictive policies causes problems for many mailing lists.

At the time of writing, the DMARC base specification had been published as Informational RFC 7489 and had seen significant deployment within the email community. Cases in which email does not flow directly from the author's administrative domain to the recipient's domains are collectively called indirect email flows. Because of existing and increasing adoption of DMARC, the impact of DMARC-based email rejection policies on indirect email flows can be significant for a select subset of general email traffic.

The issues arise when conformance to the DMARC specification leads a receiving implementation to apply DMARC-based policy restrictions to messages that are both compliant with the architecture as specified in RFC 5598 and viewed as legitimate by the intended recipient. Domains that assert a p=none policy, and messages that pass standard DMARC validation, have no interoperability issues. Messages that do not conform to IETF email specifications but are considered legitimate are not discussed.

The document presents several known causes of interoperability issues, then describes the components of the Internet Mail Architecture where they can arise, and finally presents known and possible methods for addressing them. There are often multiple ways to address any given issue, and while the document strives to be comprehensive it should not be treated as complete. It also notes that some practices in use at the time may or may not be best practices, especially as future standards evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain can ask receivers to reject its mail if it fails a security check. The check compares the domain that signed the message with the domain in the From line. Forwarded or rewritten mail breaks that comparison, so the message gets blocked even though the person who sent it would not object.

sections.title: Why the Check Fails
sections.content:
DMARC relies on DomainKeys Identified Mail in RFC 6376 and SPF in RFC 7208 to perform message source validation, and calls the source domains they validate the Authenticated Identifiers. To be used by DMARC, an Authenticated Identifier must also be related to the domain found in the message's From header field, and that relationship is called Identifier Alignment. DMARC allows alignment to be determined in two modes. Strict mode requires an exact match between the domain of any Authenticated Identifier and the From header field. Relaxed mode allows alignment when the Authenticated Identifier and the From header field share the same Organizational Domain. The interoperability issues are generally the same for both, but strict alignment constrains the possible solutions because of the more rigorous matching requirement, and some mitigations only work with relaxed alignment.

With DKIM, a signing domain must be part of the same Organizational Domain as the domain in the From header field for the identifier to align. DKIM also allows multiple valid signatures, from the same or different domains, and DMARC processes Authenticated Identifiers based on DKIM signatures until an aligned one is found. Operational experience has shown that some implementations have difficulty processing multiple signatures, and implementations that cannot process them may incorrectly flag messages as not passing alignment and apply policy to otherwise conforming messages.

SPF defines two Authenticated Identifiers per message, derived from the envelope sender domain and from the HELO or EHLO SMTP domain. The MAILFROM value is based on the envelope sender unless that value is absent, as in the case of notification messages, in which case the HELO identifier is used. This fallback definition has occasionally been misunderstood by operators, since notification messages are often an automatic feature of MTA software, and some MTA software cannot apply a DKIM signature to them.

The message format permits only one From header field, but it may contain multiple mailboxes. Because an attacker could add their domain to the From field, provide arbitrary new content and sign the message, DMARC recommends that the strictest policy be applied to such messages.

Forwarding involves the retransmission of email and introduces specific issues for SPF. If the envelope sender is present and the forwarder maintains it, SPF validation fails unless the forwarder is an authorised part of the originator's sending infrastructure; if the forwarder replaces the envelope sender with its own domain, SPF might pass but alignment with the From header field will fail. If the envelope sender is empty, as in the case of delivery status notifications, the HELO domain of the forwarder will likely be in a different Organizational Domain from the From header field's domain, so SPF may pass but alignment will fail. In both cases SPF cannot yield relevant Authenticated Identifiers, and DKIM must be relied upon.

Modification of email content invalidates most DKIM signatures, and many forwarding systems modify content. Mailing list processors are the common example. DKIM provides a length flag so that content can be appended without invalidating the signature, but in practice, particularly with MIME-encoded messages, a mailing list processor does more than simply append content, and the length flag is seldom used because of security issues. DKIM also describes two canonicalizations for preparing the header and body: simple and relaxed. The relaxed form is designed to accommodate trivial changes to whitespace and folding that generally have no semantic significance in the header, but it is more computationally intensive and may not have been preferred in the early deployment of DKIM, leaving some deployments using the less forgiving simple canonicalization. While the prevalence is unknown, there are some DKIM verifiers with problems evaluating relaxed canonicalization correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to go wrong. The signing domain may not match the From line, the message may have been forwarded so the envelope no longer points at the sender, or the message may have been edited so the signature no longer matches. Any one of them is enough for a strict policy to reject the mail.

sections.title: Where in the Mail System This Happens
sections.content:
The Internet Mail Architecture defines six basic components that make up the Message Handling System: the Message, the Message User Agent, the Message Submission Agent, the Message Transfer Agent, the Message Delivery Agent and the Message Store. It also defines a Mediator as a hybrid of several component types, which the document gives special consideration because of the unique issues they face when trying to interoperate with DMARC.

An MSA accepts messages submitted by a Message User Agent and enforces the policies of the hosting administrative domain and the requirements of Internet standards. It is split into author-focused functions and MHS-focused functions. Interoperability issues begin when an author-focused MSA accepts a message whose From header field contains a domain outside the MSA's administrative domain, which happens when someone uses a mail service with their own domain but has not configured an SPF record properly, or when a user agent tries to transmit mail as someone else, such as the forward-to-friend functionality on news sites or send-as functionality in some mail clients. When an MHS-focused MSA takes responsibility for transit of a message whose From domain is outside its administrative domain, it faces issues if that domain publishes a quarantine or reject policy. The examples given are partially open relays, embedded devices such as cable and DSL modems, firewalls, wireless access points and printers that send email using hardcoded domains, devices that send mail on behalf of a user such as scanners, security cameras and alarms, email service providers servicing customers whose domains publish a reject policy, and calendaring software where an invited attendee modifies an event and causes an update to be sent claiming to come from the creator of the event.

An MTA relays a message until it reaches a destination delivery agent, and some common message-handling strategies break the integrity of DKIM signatures, so a restrictive DMARC policy turns latent problems into overt ones. An MTA may modify the message encoding, for instance by converting 8-bit MIME sections to quoted-printable 7-bit sections, which is outside the scope of DKIM canonicalization and invalidates signatures that include message content. An MTA could also re-encode a message without changing the encoding type, producing a semantically equivalent MIME body that is not identical to the original, which is characteristic of systems that use another message representation internally. An MTA may rewrite headers to bring them into compliance with existing RFCs, for example correcting a comprehensible but non-compliant date format, which is outside the scope of DKIM canonicalization and invalidates signatures, leaving downstream DMARC processing unable to use DKIM. An MTA may also implement security-motivated changes to the content of messages, dropping or altering sections, which also breaks signatures.

An MDA transfers a message to a mailbox and, like the MSA, has MHS-focused and recipient-focused sub-components, both of which can redirect a message to an alternative address. Sieve filtering often lives in the recipient-focused part, and its addheader and deleteheader actions can modify messages and invalidate DKIM signatures; there are also Sieve extensions that modify the body, and such alterations only become an issue when the email is reintroduced into the transport infrastructure.

Mediators forward messages through a re-posting process. They share some functionality with basic relaying but have greater flexibility in addressing and content modifications, and DMARC interoperability issues are common within them, because they are often used precisely for their ability to modify messages. The DMARC design does not cope with some mediator functionality, such as content modifications that invalidate DKIM signatures and rewriting of the envelope sender to support SPF authentication of re-sent mail.

An Alias is a simple re-addressing facility that provides one or more new Internet Mail addresses rather than a single internal one, and the message continues through the transfer service to one or more alternative addresses. Aliases can be implemented by mailbox-level forwarding, by Sieve's redirect action, or by other methods. When an alias preserves message content and makes no significant header changes, DKIM signatures may remain valid, but aliases often extend the delivery path outside the scope covered by the originating administrative domain's SPF records. Examples include forwarding email between free email providers while keeping an original address, consolidating many addresses into a single account, and services offering activity-based, role-based, vanity or temporary addresses, such as universities offering an alias for the duration of a membership.

A ReSender splices a message's addressing information to connect the author of the original message with the recipients of the new message, so the new recipient sees the message as coming from the original author even if the mediator adds commentary. Without Authenticated Identifiers aligned with the author's From domain, the new recipient has no way to achieve a passing DMARC evaluation. Examples are user-agent forwarding by resending a message to a new recipient or forwarding it inline, and calendaring software that lets an attendee modify an invite so the new invitations claim to be reissued from the meeting organizer.

A Mailing List receives messages as an explicit addressee and reposts them to subscribed members, doing what can be viewed as an elaboration of the ReSender actions, and sharing the same interoperability issues. It very commonly modifies headers or content in ways that will cause DKIM to fail: prepending the Subject header with a tag, adding a footer to the body, removing MIME parts or converting the message to text only, encrypting the body with the recipient's key using PGP or S/MIME, rewriting banned words to enforce community standards, and letting moderators add arbitrary commentary. Such modifications are often central to present mailing list functionality, and mail clients have come to rely on them to present messages to users in expected ways. Mailing lists also have operational effects: subscribed members may not receive email from members who post using domains that publish a reject policy, and a list may interpret a DMARC-related rejection as an inability to deliver mail to recipients that are checking DMARC policy, which can cause subscribers that enforce DMARC to be inadvertently suspended or removed from the list.

Gateways perform the basic routing and transfer work of relaying but are also permitted to modify content, structure, addressing and other attributes to send the message into a messaging environment under different standards or incompatible policies. They share the issues of ReSenders and MTAs. Receiver systems on the non-SMTP side of a gateway may be unable to evaluate DKIM and SPF at all, and if a message passes through a second gateway back into the SMTP domain, the transformations commonly break the original signatures. Gateway-level forwarding can also introduce issues when the gateway rewrites the message into alternate receiving domains, for example when an acquiring company decides to decommission the acquired company's domains by rewriting messages to use its own domain, which invalidates signatures since the To header field is usually signed.

Boundary Filters subject messages to analysis for conformance with safety policies and may alter the content to render it safe, such as by removing unacceptable content. They share the ReSender issues, and problems arise if SPF and DKIM evaluation is performed after filter modifications. The examples are malware scanning, where an MTA removes content believed to be harmful, reformats content to canonical formats or adds text to the body noting the message has been scanned; spam filtering, where an MTA modifies a message to indicate it is likely unwanted; other text additions such as an organisational disclaimer or advertisement; URL alteration, where systems rewrite embedded URLs to control the threat from malware; and secondary MX services, where a secondary mail server outside the normal processing queues and forwards to the primary when it becomes available, which will not invalidate DKIM but will prevent the primary from validating SPF normally, so it is inappropriate for a primary to run an SPF check against its own secondaries and the secondary should instead perform it and communicate the results by a trusted mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The document walks through the mail system looking for the places that break a signature. Mail servers that re-encode or tidy headers, filters that add a footer, mailing lists that rewrite the subject line, devices that send mail under a hardcoded domain, and gateways that translate between protocols all sit on the path and can each break it.

sections.title: What Operators Are Doing About It
sections.content:
Because DMARC is already widely deployed, many operators already have mitigations in use. They vary in effectiveness and side effects but have the advantage of being available now. The document notes that mitigations may not be wanted for email of a certain category of high value or high risk, such as security-related transactional messages dealing with financial transactions or medical records, where mitigating the impact of DMARC may be counterproductive or allow abuse. Mail systems are also diverse and widely deployed, with systems of various ages and capabilities expected to preserve interoperability with the rest of the SMTP ecosystem: Qmail is still used although the base code has not been updated since 1998, and ezmlm, a once popular mailing list manager, is still deployed but has not been updated since 1997. When dealing with aging or unsupported systems, some solutions may be time-consuming or disruptive to implement.

For senders. MTAs handling multiple domains may change the envelope sender to align with the From header to improve SPF usability, and may align the HELO or EHLO with the From header, particularly when sending notification messages, though dynamically adjusting the HELO based on the From header may not be possible for some software. MTAs may sign notification messages with an aligned domain to allow a DKIM-based pass. MTAs sending on behalf of multiple domains may require domain owners to provide DKIM keys, since managing DKIM keys with a third party has security risks, though methods involving CNAMEs and subdomains may alleviate some of them. Senders acting for users in other administrative domains may use a From address under the sender's own control, either a forwarding address in a domain the sender controls or a placeholder address, with the original user's address in a Reply-To header, though this may cause the recipient's mail client to deviate from customary behaviour. For forward-to-friend functionality, one approach is to pass a well-formed message to the user's mail client so that it can fill in an appropriate identity and submit through its own submission agent. Senders can use domains with distinct DMARC policies for mail sent directly and mail known to use indirect flows, though for well-known brands all active domains are likely to be targeted equally by abusers.

Senders can also maximise the survivability of DKIM signatures by limiting the header fields they sign and using relaxed canonicalization, and by starting with compliant headers and common body formats. Using the DKIM length tag to allow appended signatures is discouraged because of the security risk of allowing arbitrary content to be appended to legitimate mail. To minimise transport-based conversions, senders can convert messages to a lowest-denominator content-transfer encoding such as quoted-printable or base64 before signing.

For receivers. Receivers should update their DKIM handling libraries to ensure they process all valid signatures and check each one for alignment. Receivers can also amalgamate data from their user base to create lists of forwarders and use those lists to inform DMARC local policy overrides, which may be easier for large receivers where data and resources are more readily available than at smaller sites.

For re-senders. Many issues can be avoided by using a From header under the re-sender's control instead of the original one, which corrects alignment and allows arbitrary modification as long as the re-sender signs the message with an aligned domain signature. When the From is changed it is desirable to preserve information about the original initiator, for instance with an Original-From header, although handling of that field is not defined anywhere, it is not used consistently or displayed to the user, and where it is used it is a new unauthenticated identifier available for exploitation unless it is included within the scope of the new signatures. Another option is to rewrite the From address to a locally controlled address that will be forwarded back to the original sender. Forwarders can also add header fields instead of modifying existing headers or bodies, can minimise the circumstances in which they fix messages, preferring to preserve non-compliant headers rather than create DKIM failures, and can choose to reject messages with suspect or harmful content instead of modifying them.

For mailing lists. Configuring the list manager to alter the From header to use the domain of the mailing list is a mitigation now present in several list software distributions. Since most subscribers prefer to know the identity of the original author, that information is typically provided in the display name part of the From header, which needs to be crafted so as not to collide with the original author's display name nor contain something that looks like an email address or domain name. These modifications may to some extent defeat the purpose of DMARC and may make it hard for users of all mail clients to reply to the author, the list or all of them; the Reply-To header field can alleviate this depending on whether the list is configured to reply to the list, to the author or to a fixed address, though that field can hold multiple addresses. When altering the From header there are three possibilities: put the mailing list's own address in it, change it to a locally defined address that forwards back to the original sender, or break the address by modifying the domain to a non-existent one such as by adding a suffix like .invalid. The last may create issues because it is an invalid domain name and some MTAs pay particular attention to the validity of addresses in the From header and to the reputation of the domains there.

Other list options are to configure the list manager to wrap the message in a MIME message/rfc822 part and send as the list's own address, though many mail clients, especially mobile ones, have difficulty reading such messages and this is not expected to change soon; to configure the manager not to modify the message so the signature remains valid, which some lists already do and which requires few additional changes, though moving lists that currently modify mail to such a policy may be too much of a change for their members; and to reject posts or membership requests from domains with a policy other than p=none, which members may complain about as unfair exclusion. To alleviate unsubscribes caused by messages bouncing because of DMARC, the list manager needs not to act on notification messages due to message authentication issues, and correctly interpreting extended SMTP error messages is useful, since enhanced status codes for SPF and DKIM causes are defined in RFC 7372 and DMARC-related failure indications are discussed in the DMARC specification. All these techniques may create specific challenges for mail clients and for end-user workflows such as rules that sort mail into folders, and there will be some time before all the implications are understood.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixes are mostly practical: sign the message with a domain the list controls, do not touch the message if you can avoid it, and if you must change it, sign it again. The document warns that some of these choices partly defeat the point of DMARC, and that the trade-off should be thought about for important mail such as bank or medical messages.

sections.title: Work Still in Progress
sections.content:
Section 4.2 lists mitigations based on Internet-Drafts that are still in process, described as an exploratory path for solutions that should not be used in a production environment. Because drafts are transient, no specific citations are given; those that gain consensus will become RFCs.

The list covers third-party authorisation schemes that provide ways to extend Identifier Alignment under the control of the domain owner; ways to canonicalize messages that transit mailing lists so that their alterations can be isolated from the original signed content; mechanisms to record the message transformations applied at each hop so they can be reversed and the original signed content recovered; conditional DKIM signatures, where the author's domain indicates its signature is only good if accompanied by a signature from an expected downstream relay; and mechanisms to extend the Authentication-Results header field to multiple hops, creating a provable chain of custody as well as a view of message authentication results at each handling step.

Section 4.2.1 goes further. A number of operators are using strict alignment mode in DMARC in order to avoid receiving new and innovative forms of unwanted and unauthentic email through systems purporting to be mailing list handlers. The receiving administrative domain has no knowledge of which lists the user has subscribed to and which they have not. One avenue of exploration would be for the user to authorise mailing lists as proxies for authentication, at which point the receiving domain would be vesting some trust in the mailing list service. The creators of DKIM foresaw precisely this possibility by not tightly binding any semantics to the From header field, and some experimental work has taken place in this area. Additional work might examine a new communication path to the user to authorise some form of transitive trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Longer-term fixes are still being drafted. They include letting a list act on the author's behalf with the author's permission, recording what each hop did to the message so it can be undone, and signing mail only when the next hop also signs it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is an analysis of DMARC's impact on indirect email flows, and describes the possibility of accidental denial of service that can be created by rejections of messages by DMARC-aware mail receivers. It points back to the discussion of appropriate DKIM key management in the face of third-party senders, and warns that rewriting the From header field to create an artificial domain name should not be done with any domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Two cautions. Strict checking can block mail by accident, which is a denial of service in effect. And a list that invents a fake From domain is a bad idea.

viz.caption: The components of the Message Handling System and the mediators

children.label: Message User Agent
children.note: Where a person reads and writes mail.

children.label: Message Transfer Agent
children.note: Relays the message to the destination.

children.label: Message Delivery Agent
children.note: Moves the message into a mailbox; may apply Sieve rules.

children.label: Message Store
children.note: Where the delivered message is kept.

children.label: Mediators
children.note: Hybrids that re-post messages, with more freedom to change them.

viz.caption: What forwarding and modification do to the two checks

cells: The forwarder keeps the original envelope sender
Fails, unless the forwarder is an authorised part of the originator's sending infrastructure.
Signatures survive, since the signed content is unchanged.
The forwarder replaces the envelope sender with its own domain
May pass, but the domain no longer aligns with the From header field.
Signatures survive, since the signed content is unchanged.
A notification message with an empty envelope sender
Uses the HELO domain of the forwarder, which is usually in a different Organizational Domain.
Survives only if the software can sign notification messages at all.
The message content or headers are modified
Invalidated, because the signed content no longer matches.

viz.caption: The four groups of mitigation the document describes

items.title: For senders
items.text: Align the envelope sender or HELO with the From header, sign notification messages, use relaxed canonicalization, and sign in a lowest-common-denominator encoding before sending.

items.title: For receivers
items.text: Process all valid DKIM signatures and check each for alignment, and build lists of known forwarders to drive local policy overrides.

items.title: For re-senders
items.text: Use a From address under your own control and sign it, add header fields rather than editing the message, and reject suspect mail rather than rewriting it.

items.title: For mailing lists
items.text: Change the From to the list's own domain, or leave the message untouched so the signature survives, or reject posts from domains with a policy other than p=none.
